newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish forces hit home at Erbakan in Islamist row.
newsitem.headline: Turkish forces hit home at Erbakan in Islamist row.

text.p: Turkey's secularist security establishment, encouraged by the weakening of the Islamist-led government, took a campaign against religious activism straight to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's front door on Monday.
A quasi-military court began hearing a case against the preacher at a mosque in the courtyard of Erbakan's Welfare Party headquarters, the state-run Anatolian news agency said.
And police officials said they had closed down more than 20 buildings in two western districts where Islamists were teaching Koranic lessons without licences.
The ruling alliance took a body blow at the weekend when two anti-Islamist ministers resigned in protest at Erbakan's failure to curtail a religious upsurge, as demanded by the military.
But Erbakan's secularist coalition partner has stood by him.
Anatolian said mosque preacher Ali Kucuker faces up to three years in jail if found guilty of spreading hatred in a speech at Friday prayers in the Hamidiye mosque on February 14.
"In his speech, the accused advocated the principle of Sharia (Islamic law) and said the people were divided into groups of Moslems and secularists," it said.
Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, and the Welfare leadership often worship at Kucuker's mosque.
Police raided seven buildings in the western province of Bursa at the weekend in a push against outlawed Koranic courses.
"The courses were closed," a spokesman for Bursa governor's officer told Reuters. "They were found to be operating outside the writ of the religious affairs directorate," he said.
The raids were the first confirmed report of concrete action since the army demanded two months ago they were to be stamped out under a crackdown against a religious revival.
Erbakan attempts to stall the army has angered many MPs in the government ally True Path Party.
Their party leader, Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, on Monday reiterated her commitment to the government. "We will continue to work with stability," she told reporters after talks with Erbakan.
Ciller, a U.S.-educated technocrat who was Turkey's first woman prime minister, says she is better placed to persuade the prime minister to toe the army's line from within the coalition.
Erbakan signed a communique issued by the military-dominated National Security Council on Saturday agreeing to go ahead with curbs on the role of Islam in public life.
However, senior Welfare MPs have vowed to block any bid by parliament to restrict religious education, a key army demand.
A senior military officer voiced the generals' growing frustration at Erbakan's failure to heed their orders.

"The prime minister accepts everything in the National Security Council and says he agrees but then (Erbakan's Welfare Party) RP spokesmen outside say the complete opposite," the officer was quoted as saying in the Milliyet daily.

He accused Erbakan of "takkiye", a practice under which Moslems may hide their true feelings for the good of the faith. "Erbakan is practising takkiye. He is trying to form a trap, play for time," he said.
Shares in Istanbul closed down 1.71 percent on concerns over the future of Erbakan's 10-month-old administration.
The market, highly sensitive to Turkey's almost endemic political instability, lost 4.9 percent in one day last week after a press report that Ciller would abandon the coalition.

The military believes religious secondary schools, which would be marginalised under proposed education reforms, are producing a new breed of Islamists ready to infiltrate the secularist establishment.
The generals also say illegal Koranic courses, mostly prevalent in poor neighborhoods, openly encourage children to fight secularism.
